present_on_scene_date.note: PRESENCE ON THE SCENE DATE IS AN ASSUMPTION OF CONTINUITY AND NOT A STATEMENT. Nothing reached follows this household past 1833. It is graded uncertain rather than present because the town's population roughly quadrupled between the roster and the scene date and a great many of the men on it were, in Andreas's own phrase, 'adventurers, comprising moneyed speculators and prospectors, as yet undecided whether to stay at Chicago or go on'.

occupation.note: 'David Carver, seaman and lumber merchant, came in 1833.' Two trades in one clause; lumber merchant is the one that describes a resident business and seaman is recorded in the note.

persons.note: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'. It gives a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, and it is a retrospective of 1884: a YEAR off it is documented, a MONTH is not, and it says nothing whatever about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Carver, David” (poll_1833_007, line 28); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Carver, David” (tax_1833_013, line 65); Poll list of 1835 — “Carver, David” (poll_1835_014, line 299). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Carver' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

research_note: A SEAMAN AND A LUMBER MERCHANT, WHICH IS ONE MAN DESCRIBING THE WHOLE ECONOMY. Every stick of sawn lumber in the 1835 town came in by water - the lumber for St Mary's came by scow from St Joseph at $12 per thousand, hauled up from the schooner by Anson Taylor's team - and this is the household that connects the two ends of that trade. He was one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833. THE ONE SAW-MILL THE SOURCES MENTION IS DISPUTED: Andreas puts one on the North Branch below Clybourne's at the mouth of a slough just south of Division Street and prints a footnote against himself - 'John Cass says there was no mill there.'

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
